entries.content: "Bad company corrupts good character": This quote comes from the Greek poet Menander, who lived in the 300s BC. Paul uses it as a warning not to follow or listen to people who teach what is false.

entries.title: 1 Corinthians
entries.content: some of you are ignorant of God: Paul strongly criticizes those who are proud of their knowledge but doubt the resurrection.

entries.title: 1 Corinthians
entries.content: Paul talks about what resurrection bodies are like, possibly answering doubts. In the Greco-Roman world, people often believed the soul was immortal, but not that the body could rise again.

entries.title: 1 Corinthians
entries.content: You fool!: Paul’s strong response suggests skepticism. It might also imply that the answer cannot be known.

entries.title: 1 Corinthians
entries.content: Just as a plant's shape does not look like its seed, the seed still determines the plant's growth. Similarly, the resurrection body will differ from the current body but will still be recognizable as the same person.

entries.title: 1 Corinthians
entries.content: Everything God has made has its own glory. This means each thing has its own beauty and greatness. The resurrection body will also be different. It will not be like anything else.

entries.title: 1 Corinthians
entries.content: Resurrection bodies will be very different from our mortal bodies, just as plants differ from the seeds they grow from.

entries.title: 1 Corinthians
entries.content: Just as Christ's life-giving Spirit goes beyond natural life, the spiritual body will replace the physical body.

entries.title: 1 Corinthians
entries.content: Adam and Christ created two different groups of people. One group is natural and earthly, bound by sin and death. The other group is spiritual and heavenly, cleansed and meant for life. Adam symbolizes the natural, physical body, while Christ represents the spiritual, resurrected body. See also 1 Corinthians 15:21–22; Romans 5:12–21.

entries.title: 1 Corinthians
entries.content: Adam was made from the dust of the earth (Genesis 2:7), showing his earthly origin. This contrasts with Christ's heavenly origin.

entries.title: 1 Corinthians
entries.content:
• Earthly man: Like Adam, natural human beings face the curse of sin and death. All return to dust (see Genesis 3:19). They all die. 

• as is the heavenly man, so also are those who are of heaven: Those who belong to Christ share in his eternal spiritual life.

entries.title: 1 Corinthians
entries.content: Like Adam, the first man, we have physical bodies in this life. But one day, we will be like Christ, the heavenly man, and experience the kingdom of God with resurrection bodies (compare Romans 6:4–14).

entries.title: 1 Corinthians
entries.content: Physical bodies cannot enter God's kingdom. Only a spiritual, resurrected body can fully experience the kingdom (compare John 4:24).

entries.title: 1 Corinthians
entries.content:
• The good news about Jesus reveals the once unknown secret of resurrection. 

• We will not all sleep: Paul might have expected the future resurrection during his own lifetime (compare 1 Corinthians 15:52; 1 Thessalonians 4:15, 1 Thessalonians 4:17).

entries.title: 1 Corinthians
entries.content: Compare 1 Thessalonians 4:13–17

entries.title: 1 Corinthians
entries.content: "Death has been swallowed up in victory": Resurrection defeats the ultimate enemy, death. The power of the Spirit helps believers overcome sin now (see Romans 8:2, Romans 8:11).

entries.title: 1 Corinthians
entries.content:
• This quote from (Hosea 13:14 assures believers they need not fear death. 

• Death is compared to the sting of a scorpion.

entries.title: 1 Corinthians
entries.content: The death and resurrection of Christ end the control of sin and death (see Romans 6:14; Romans 8:2; Romans 10:4).

entries.title: 1 Corinthians
entries.content: your labor in the Lord is not in vain: Those who serve him faithfully will receive eternal rewards (see 1 Corinthians 3:12–15).

entries.title: 1 Corinthians
entries.content: Galatia was a Roman province in Asia Minor, modern-day Turkey (see Acts 16:6; Acts 18:23).

entries.title: 1 Corinthians
entries.content: Paul responds to the Corinthians' question about the donation for poor Christians in Jerusalem (Acts 24:17; Romans 15:25–27; Second Corinthians 8–9; Galatians 2:10).

entries.title: 1 Corinthians
entries.content: Christians gathered on the first day of each week (see Acts 20:7) instead of the last day, as in the Old Testament (Exodus 20:8; Exodus 34:21; Isaiah 58:13–14). The first day was called the "Lord's Day," marking the day of the Lord's resurrection (Mark 16:9; Luke 24:13–15; John 20:19; Revelation 1:10). The amount of money to give was not specified. Paul later encouraged them to give as generously as possible (2 Corinthians 8:1–4; 2 Corinthians 9:6–13; compare Luke 12:33–34; Luke 21:1–4; 1 Timothy 6:18–19).

entries.title: 1 Corinthians
entries.content: Paul delivered the gift to Jerusalem (Romans 15:25–26).

entries.title: 1 Corinthians
entries.content:
• Paul traveled through Macedonia, a Roman province in northern Greece, during his second missionary journey (Acts 15:36–18:22). 

• He planned to travel through Macedonia again (See Acts 19:21; Acts 20:1–3).

entries.title: 1 Corinthians
entries.content: or even spend the winter: Paul evidently did visit during the winter (compare Acts 20:2–3).

entries.title: 1 Corinthians
entries.content:
• Paul wrote this letter while he was in Ephesus, around AD 53 to 56 (Acts 19:1–20:1). 

• Pentecost occurred in May or June.

entries.title: 1 Corinthians
entries.content:
• If Timothy comes: See 1 Corinthians 4:17. Timothy was Paul's spiritual child and co-worker (see 1 Timothy 1:2). 

• see to it that he has nothing to fear: Timothy might have been shy or tentative (2 Timothy 1:6–8).

entries.title: 1 Corinthians
entries.content: our brother Apollos: Refer to study note on 1 Corinthians 1:12.

entries.title: 1 Corinthians
entries.content: Stephanas, Fortunatus, and Achaicus traveled from Corinth to visit Paul in Ephesus (see also 1 Corinthians 1:16; 1 Corinthians 16:15).

entries.title: 1 Corinthians
entries.content:
• Aquila and Priscilla (also called Prisca in Greek) had moved from Corinth to Ephesus, where Paul wrote this letter (compare Acts 18:1–3). 

• the church that meets at their house: Aquila and Priscilla later continued this practice in Rome (see Romans 16:3–5).

entries.title: 1 Corinthians
entries.content: Like in his other letters, Paul greets his friends and offers a blessing.

entries.title: 1 Corinthians
entries.content: Greet one another with a holy kiss: People often greeted each other with a kiss on the cheek.

entries.title: 1 Corinthians
entries.content: Paul ends the letter by writing a few words in his own handwriting. In those times, it was common for someone else to write down the letter as a secretary. Paul did this in this letter and in others (see Romans 16:22; Galatians 6:11; Colossians 4:18; 2 Thessalonians 3:17).

entries.title: 1 Corinthians
entries.content:
• To be cursed means to be condemned by God (see also Romans 9:3; Galatians 1:8–9). 

• Come, O Lord!: Early Christians sometimes used this phrase in prayers (see also Revelation 22:20).

entries.title: 1 Corinthians
entries.content:
• All of Paul's letters end with a blessing like this one. 

• Paul mentions grace at both the start and end of this letter (see 1 Corinthians 1:3).
